Welcome! This workshop is intended to provide learners with an introduction to key challenges and threats in scientific research. It explores different forms of research bias, statistical uncertainties, and common sources of errors that can affect the reliability and reproducibility of research findings. Through practical examples and research scenarios, the workshop encourages critical analysis of questionable research practices and their impact on scientific integrity. It also reflects on current systemic challenges in research culture and discusses the importance of developing more transparent and robust approaches to conducting and evaluating research.

Who are these materials for?

Educators in higher education with or without familiarity with open research planning to teach open research to novices
Self-learners with no or limited familiarity with open research planning to develop and build up on their open research skills

title: Educational resources for teaching open research to novices
text:
What materials are there?
The materials consist of slide decks with theoretical elements, hands-on exercises, cheatsheets, homework assignments and practical tips on the content.
Each slide deck on a given topic is designed for a 90-minute session in a classroom setting (in-person, virtual, or hybrid), and can be flexibly adapted depending on your audience and timeframe.
Detailed presenter notes (intended narrative of the presentation), further instructor notes (additional guidance intended only for the presenter) and accessibility tips (where applicable) are available for each topic and are directly integrated into the materials.
The materials are completely free to use, given that you give appropriate credit.






TipAdapting the materials





You want to adapt the materials for your audience? The source code for the materials as well as PowerPoint files are available for download to tailor the materials to your exact audience.

title: Educational resources for teaching open research to novices
section: How can I use these materials?
text:
How can I use these materials?
As an educator aiming to teach about open research: The materials are ready for immediate use in a classroom setting (timeframe: approx. 90 minutes per topic). You can choose to deliver a full course with the existing materials, or you can pick-and-choose specific open research topics to incorporate into an existing course. To access the materials, use the navigation menu on the left. The materials are arranged in a chronological order, meaning that they logically build up on one another. The slides can be directly presented in the browser in full screen or can be downloaded as pdf or MS PowerPoint if you want to edit them or present the materials offline. Presenter notes, instructor notes and accessibility tips provide important information about the content of the materials and valuable pedagogical tips on how to convey the materials to your audience. If you opt for the pick-and-choose option, make sure to thoroughly read the prerequisites for each topic and go through the content and exercises yourself. If you re-use the materials for your own teaching, make sure to give appropriate credit to the original authors.
As a self-learner: Select your topic of choice from the navigation menu on the left. Follow along the slides and complete the practical exercises in your own time. You can navigate the slides in full screen using the arrow key, or by viewing the slides in the Speaker View together with the presenter and instructor notes to understand and reflect on the content of the materials (recommended, see here for more information). Make sure to always familiarize yourself with the prerequisites before starting a new topic. The materials can be downloaded as pdf or MS PowerPoint documents. Note: Group exercises are not possible in an asynchronous setting, but can be completed individually.






ImportantRead the introductory page for each topic





When selecting a topic, you will be redirected to a separate website with all the materials. Please ensure to read the About these materials section, as well as details about the intended target audience, the prerequisites to complete the topic and the learning objectives. You can also find the contributor list, the license details and the citation statement on each website.

How can I adapt the materials?
Of course, the context in which you are teaching may vary greatly and you may need to adapt the materials in terms of your audience, content, level of difficulty or timeframe. If you want to adapt the materials, you can export the slides as MS PowerPoint (.pptx format) corresponding to the materials and adapt the materials to your specific teaching context. Make sure to give appropriate credit to the original authors. You also have the option to export the slides in pdf format.
In addition, you can also obtain the materials from our LMU OSC GitHub repository. You can clone and fork the repository to adapt the materials to your needs, or create a new branch to work on the materials in parallel. Within this repository, you have direct access to the Quarto .qmd files that support all of our materials.

title: Educational resources for teaching open research to novices
text:
Frequently asked questions

What previous knowledge do I need about open research to teach with those slides?


No prior open research knowledge is required! You can first acquire the open research skills yourself by going through the slides and practical activities, or you can also complete the self-paced tutorials on these topics in the self learning catalogue. In addition, you can develop your teaching skills here.


Who can I teach with these materials?


The materials can be flexibly adapted to bachelor students, master students or early career researchers (PhD, PostDocs) who are new to open research or have not had prior training on these topics.


I am not a member of the LMU Open Science Center, can I still teach with these slides?


Yes! Just make sure to give the appropriate credit and honor the licence conditions while teaching (this also applies to LMU-based educators!). If you are based at LMU, consider joining the LMU Open Science Center to support the goal of open, responsible, and reproducible research within your disciplines or at LMU Munich more broadly.

[Example text for Quarto] Welcome! This workshop is intended to introduce Quarto, an open-source publishing system that allows users to combine text, code, and other outputs to create reproducible reports, presentations, and websites. Learners will experience the basic workflow of creating and editing Quarto documents, rendering them into different formats, and using Quarto within an R-based research workflow. Learners will focus on practicing different Quarto elements to structure documents, include analysis results, and control the appearance of their outputs. In addition, the session demonstrates how to add citations and automatically generate a bibliography using Zotero. Through this guided, hands-on tutorial, learners will create their own Quarto document, render it into a finished output, and learn how to publish and share their work online using GitHub Pages. ### Who are these materials for?

Educators in higher education with or without familiarity with open research planning to teach open research to novices
Self-learners with no or limited familiarity with open research planning to develop and build up on their open research skills
